text:
A: Hiya, you alright? I'm Callum.
B: Hello. Yes, fine, thank you. I'm Hira.
A: Nice one. Sorry, I've only just sat back down, I was making a tea. Where abouts are you?
B: Reading. Earley, actually, just outside.
A: Oh right, yeah. I'm Sittingbourne, in Kent. Not too far, sort of, just the other side of London.
B: Okay. I don't know Kent very well. Only passing through, I think.
A: Most people only pass through, to be fair. Did you get on alright with the puzzle bit?
B: Erm, I think so. I was a bit slow. I like to check things twice, so I didn't finish the last one.
A: Yeah, same, I ran out of time on the last one. I was sort of going round in circles. So what do you do, if you don't mind me asking?
B: I work in a hospital pharmacy. On the wards, mostly.
A: Oh, nice. That's a proper job, that. That's important stuff.
B: It's okay. It's a lot of checking. What about you?
A: Erm, I'm a machine operator at a cardboard box place. Corrugated packaging. I run a printer that prints and folds and glues the boxes, and I do the setups when we change orders over. Rotating shifts, so days one week and backs the next. It's not glamorous, but I like it, you know. You know where you are with a machine. Mostly.
B: That sounds quite precise, actually. If one setting is wrong, the whole batch is wrong.
A: Yeah, exactly that. You do your checks first or you end up with two thousand boxes in the bin. Bit like your job, I suppose, but with nobody getting hurt.
B: Yes. We are a bit like that. A small mistake, and then it matters.
A: Do you have to get in early and that?
B: Before eight, which is the problem, because the car park is a nightmare. If you're five minutes late there's no space at all.
A: Oh, I feel that. For me it's the A249. You get one lorry break down and that's it, everyone's sat there.
B: Same thing, different road.
A: Pretty much, yeah. What do you get up to outside work, then?
B: Erm, I walk quite a lot, by the river. I crochet. And I have some plants in pots in the back yard. Chillies, coriander, mint.
A: No way, chillies? I grow chillies. I've got raised beds in the garden, I built them myself, and it's tomatoes, chillies and runner beans mostly. How have yours done this year?
B: Surprisingly well, actually. I didn't expect it. I think it was the warm few weeks in July.
A: That's what I reckon. Mine have gone mad. It's the tomatoes I'm worried about. Half of them are still green and the weather's turning, so it's a bit touch and go, you know.
B: My mother-in-law puts the green ones on the windowsill. I think they ripen there.
A: Yeah, my mum does that. Only problem is our cat, Biscuit. Anything on the windowsill, he just knocks it straight off. Looks right at you while he does it, too.
B: Acha, so the tomatoes are not safe.
A: Nothing's safe, mate. Sorry, I mean, nothing is. What sort of chillies have you got, then?
B: Erm, just a green one, the small kind. My mum uses them, so I wanted the same. I put them in daal, mostly.
A: Oh, that'd be nice. I mostly just chuck mine in a chilli, to be honest. Megan, my wife, says I put too many in, but-
